title: Discrete Entropy: Measuring Uncertainty
hook: How many bits does it take to describe the outcome of a random experiment? Change the probabilities and see.

equation.caption: Entropy of a discrete probability distribution.

compute: function compute(inputs){ const raw = inputs.probs.slice(0, inputs.n); const sumRaw = raw.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0); let p = raw.map(x=> x/sumRaw); if(sumRaw===0){ p = raw.map(()=> 1/raw.length); } const contributions = p.map(pi => pi>0 ? -pi*Math.log2(pi) : 0); const H = contributions.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0); const tableRows = p.map((pi,i)=> [i+1, pi, pi>0 ? -Math.log2(pi) : 0, contributions[i]]); const maxH = Math.log2(p.length); const insight = `Entropy = ${H.toFixed(3)} bits. Maximum for ${p.length} outcomes is ${maxH.toFixed(3)} bits.`; return { H, p, contributions, table: { columns: ['Outcome','p_i','-log2 p_i','Contribution'], rows: tableRows }, insight }; }
steps: For each outcome, compute self-information: -\log_2 p_i

explorations.title: Certainty vs. Uncertainty
explorations.predict: If one outcome has probability 1, what is the entropy?
explorations.observe: Entropy is 0 bits. The table shows only one non-zero contribution.
explorations.why: When p_i=1, -p_i log2 p_i = 0, and all other terms are 0 (since 0 log 0 = 0). So H=0.

explorations.title: Equally Likely Outcomes
explorations.predict: If four outcomes are equally likely, what is the entropy?
explorations.why: Each outcome has p_i=1/4, so -log2(1/4)=2, and each contributes 0.25*2=0.5. Summing four gives 2 bits.

limitation: This model assumes outcomes are independent and identically distributed; it does not capture entropy of sequences with memory or continuous variables.
misconception: Entropy is not the number of outcomes; it depends on their probabilities. A certain outcome has zero entropy.

claims.text: Entropy is defined as H = -\sum p_i \log_2 p_i.
For a uniform distribution over n outcomes, H = \log_2 n.
Our toy uses up to 4 outcomes and normalizes probabilities automatically.

outcomes.outcome: Compute entropy from a probability distribution.
Explain why certainty gives zero bits.
Show that four equally likely outcomes give two bits.
